questions.q: What is the relationship between debate, recursive reward modeling, and weak-to-strong generalization, according to this lesson?
options: They are three unrelated techniques with no common strategy behind them
They are three specific instances of the broader strategy of AI-assisted human oversight — using AI tools to extend what a human can reliably judge
They are three names for exactly the same technique
They are competing techniques, and only one of them is considered valid by researchers
questions.explain: Each technique extends human judgment in a different way, but all three fall under the same general strategy of AI-assisted human oversight.

questions.q: What did OpenAI's research on self-critiquing models find?
options: Showing a human a model-generated critique alongside an answer helped human evaluators catch more flaws than reading the answer alone
Critique models always produce worse evaluation outcomes than no assistance at all
Human evaluators ignored critiques entirely and performance was unaffected
Critique models eliminated the need for any human evaluation whatsoever
questions.explain: This was a direct, measurable instance of AI assistance expanding what a human overseer could reliably notice in an output.

questions.q: What does the "sandwiching" experimental method measure?
options: Whether a model can be squeezed between two other models during training
Whether AI assistance lets a group of non-expert humans approach the judgments of genuine domain experts on a task
The physical size of a model's parameter count relative to its training data
Whether two AI debaters agree with each other more often than they disagree
questions.explain: Sandwiching tests a real capability gap — non-experts assisted by AI versus true experts — to see whether the assistance technique closes meaningful ground.

questions.q: Does this lesson claim that scalable oversight is now a fully solved problem?
options: Yes, all three techniques covered in this chapter have fully solved scalable oversight
No — it explicitly describes debate's obfuscated-argument concern, recursive reward modeling's reliability dependence, and weak-to-strong generalization's partial recovery as still-open limitations
Yes, because self-critiquing models eliminate every known limitation
No, because none of the techniques in this chapter have ever been tested empirically
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this chapter represents real but partial progress, not a claim that scalable oversight has been fully solved.

questions.q: According to this lesson's framing, what is the shared underlying question all AI-assisted human oversight techniques try to answer?
options: How to remove humans from the evaluation process entirely as quickly as possible
How to keep a human meaningfully in the loop on a task that has outgrown what the human can check alone
How to make AI models cheaper to run in production
How to guarantee a model never makes any mistakes during training
questions.explain: Every technique in this family is a different proposed way to extend meaningful human oversight to tasks beyond unaided human verification ability.
